name: Marco Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: First thing I do is check my phone before my boots are on, because the pig shed sensors send me the temperature and water use overnight. We've got about four hundred finishing pigs, that's pigs we grow from young to market weight, and sixty hectares of wheat and beans on the farm off Station Road. My wife Lucia is a nurse at the district hospital, so mornings are a scramble with the kids. I love the problem-solving, figuring out why one pen is eating less, and I'm worn out by how little control we have over the price at the end.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned sensors. Do you use AI tools too?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I ask a chat program to explain new rules from the ministry in plain words, I use it to plan the spraying on the wheat, and I've built a little spreadsheet that it helps me check. Lucia teases me that I talk to it more than to her. I'm the guy at the pig meetings everyone asks about gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great tool and more farmers should use it, I'd probably post a little video on how I use it for spray plans. I'd also say the useful stuff should be free and open, not locked up by two big companies. That's my usual speech, people know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a little disappointed. I like this stuff and I hoped it would do more. But for the family it's fine: pigs still need feeding, Lucia's job is safe, the mortgage is the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and push a bit further. I'd try one of the camera systems that weigh pigs by looking at them, about three thousand, so I know exactly when to send them to market. And I'd run a free evening at the village hall to show other farmers the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. Like waiting for a storm that turns into drizzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you want it free and open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the last time farmers got clever machines, the tractor companies locked them so you can't fix them yourself. I've had a tractor sit dead for a week waiting for a dealer to plug in a laptop. I don't want the same thing with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who'd come to your evening at the hall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger ones, and a couple of older guys who'd come just to tell me it's all nonsense. That's fine, I'd put the kettle on. Old Bernard came last time and now he uses the weather app every day, he'd never admit it.

S0.say: It's a great tool and more farmers should use it, but the useful stuff should be free and open. It shouldn't be locked up by two big companies.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed, because I hoped it would do more. For the family it's fine: the pigs still need feeding, Lucia's job is safe and the mortgage is the same.
S0.do: Tries a camera system that weighs pigs by sight for about three thousand, to time market sales better. Runs a free evening at the village hall to show other farmers the tools.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a storm that turned into drizzle.
S0.quote: I've had a tractor sit dead for a week waiting for a dealer to plug in a laptop. I don't want the same thing with AI.
S0.fieldNote: He was the only farmer so far who seemed let down that AI stays small. His enthusiasm comes with a sharp political edge about ownership and the right to repair. The story of old Bernard secretly using the weather app shows he enjoys converting sceptics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a chance to plan it properly, with public money for training and farmer co-ops owning the kit. I'd say companies hiring fewer beginners is a scandal and they should be made to train people. I'd say that online and at the pig producers' meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it's good. I'm already ahead, so a slow change gives me an edge for longer. But I think about Lucia's ward, they're always short-staffed, and if hospitals hire fewer young nurses because computers do the notes, that's a disaster for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get three or four neighbours together to share a field robot for weeding the beans, splitting maybe twenty thousand between us. I'd take a short online course in data for farming, about two evenings a week. And I'd keep the pig weighing cameras, they'd have paid for themselves by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a bit of worry for Lucia's colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your neighbours really share a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two would, maybe three. Hans would, he hates hoeing. Others would say what if it breaks on your field and mine's waiting? So we'd need a simple rota and a written agreement, which, to be honest, I'd get the chat program to draft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it gives you an edge. Isn't that a bit at odds with sharing it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I see it. I like being first, I won't pretend I don't. But I'd rather be first in a co-op than first on my own with a loan I can't pay.

S1.say: Ten years is a chance to plan it properly, with public training money and farmer co-ops owning the kit. Companies hiring fewer beginners should be made to train people.
S1.think: A slow change is good for me, because I'm already ahead and keep an edge for longer. But if hospitals hire fewer young nurses, that's a disaster for Lucia's ward.
S1.do: Gets three or four neighbours to share a weeding robot for the beans, splitting about twenty thousand. Takes an online course in farm data two evenings a week and keeps the pig-weighing cameras.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with some worry for his wife's colleagues.
S1.quote: I like being first, I won't pretend I don't. But I'd rather be first in a co-op than first on my own with a loan I can't pay.
S1.fieldNote: I named the tension between his wish to be ahead and his belief in sharing, and he admitted it cheerfully. His caution with money shows despite his love of gadgets: he'd split costs rather than borrow. His wife's hospital ward is where he feels the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need strong unions and a proper plan, not politicians shouting. Office workers are being treated like a cost to cut. I'd post a long thread about it, and I'd mean every word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a lot of the pig business is office work, the contracts, the paperwork with the processor, the vet records. If that goes automatic, the processor gets faster and leaner and they'll squeeze me on price. But I also think I could use the same tools to fight back, check their numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use an AI assistant to go through every contract with the processor, compare the price per kilo against the market, and find where they've been shaving. I'd join the pig producers' committee, so I'm in the room. And I'd ask Lucia whether the hospital's new note-taking system is actually helping or just cutting staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but fired up. Like before a match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if you found the processor shaving the price?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Share it with the committee first, then with the farming paper. Last year I found they'd changed how they measure lean meat and it cost us about two per pig. On four hundred pigs that's a holiday gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want one of the new AI jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part-time, maybe. Helping a farm advisory service set these tools up for farmers, I'd enjoy that. But I'd keep the pigs, I'm not leaving the farm for a desk.

S2.say: This is why we need strong unions and a proper plan, not politicians shouting. Office workers are being treated like a cost to cut.
S2.think: The pig business has a lot of office work, and a leaner processor will squeeze me on price. But I could use the same tools to fight back and check their numbers.
S2.do: Uses an AI assistant to check every processor contract against market prices per kilo and joins the pig producers' committee. Asks Lucia whether the hospital's new note-taking system helps or just cuts staff.
S2.feel: Anxious but fired up, like before a match.
S2.quote: Last year I found they'd changed how they measure lean meat and it cost us about two per pig. On four hundred pigs that's a holiday gone.
S2.fieldNote: He sees AI as a weapon for small farmers against the big processor, not just a threat. His stories are full of numbers and he plainly enjoys the fight. He would take a part-time AI advisory role but won't leave the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a real windfall tax and public ownership of a share of the AI companies. If house prices are booming while professionals lose jobs, the system is broken. I'd be out marching and I'd bring the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the farm is fairly safe here, physical work stays. But I'd worry about the price of land going up with everything else, because I rent twenty of my hectares and the landlord would want more. And Lucia, if AI matches doctors at diagnosis, the nurses might get more work, not less, or they might get squeezed, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to buy those twenty rented hectares before the price runs away, if the bank would lend, or at least lock in a five-year lease. I'd use the tools even more to cut costs on feed. And I'd offer to help a couple of laid-off office people from the village with a farm job, if they wanted one, because we need hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Angry at the unfairness, safe-ish in my own boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really hire someone who'd just lost an office job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. My cousin Paolo was an accountant, and if he lost his job I'd have him mucking out by Monday, and doing my books by Wednesday. People think farm work is unskilled, but you learn it, and some office people would love being outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids at the march?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's not about hating computers. It's about who gets the money they make. My son is nine, he'd probably just want a hot dog, but he'd remember being there.

S3.say: This is the moment for a windfall tax and public ownership of a share of the AI companies. If house prices boom while professionals lose jobs, the system is broken.
S3.think: The farm is fairly safe, but the twenty hectares I rent would get dearer as land prices rise. For Lucia's nursing, I honestly don't know whether it means more work or a squeeze.
S3.do: Tries to buy the twenty rented hectares, or at least lock in a five-year lease, before prices run away. Cuts feed costs with AI tools and offers farm work to laid-off office people from the village.
S3.feel: Uneasy and angry at the unfairness, while feeling fairly safe in his own work.
S3.quote: My cousin Paolo was an accountant, and if he lost his job I'd have him mucking out by Monday, and doing my books by Wednesday.
S3.fieldNote: He saw rising land prices as his main risk here, which other farmers might miss. He was honest that he didn't know what the change meant for his wife's nursing. His offer to hire laid-off office workers came across as both kind and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the robots should belong to the people who use them, the farm co-ops, not the companies selling them by subscription. And I'd say farm workers who lose jobs need a guaranteed income while they retrain. I'd say it everywhere, and I'd run the meetings myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's both the best and worst news. Robots in the pig shed could clean and check the animals all night, which I'd love. But a big pig company with five sheds and a hundred robots would make pork cheaper than I ever can, and I'd be finished on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. I'd get the co-op to buy two or three robots together and rent them to members, starting with the weeding and the pig cleaning, and I'd put in maybe ten thousand of my own savings, which is a lot for us. I'd also look at selling some pork direct, as higher-welfare, because that's where the big companies can't follow. And I'd tell Lucia we're taking a risk, and get her agreement first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and excited at once. Like riding a bike downhill with no brakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Lucia say, in your head, when you told her about the ten thousand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, Marco, that's our emergency money, what happens if the roof goes? And she'd be right. We'd agree on five, and I'd find the other five from somewhere else, probably by selling the old trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the tools every day. Does the robot picture scare you at all, personally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, actually. Not the robot, but the thought that someday I'm the one who isn't needed, just checking a screen. I farm because I like being in the shed with the pigs, I don't want to farm from my phone.

S4.say: Robots should belong to the farm co-ops that use them, not to companies renting them out by subscription. Farm workers who lose jobs need a guaranteed income while they retrain.
S4.think: It's both the best and worst news: robots could clean and check the pigs all night. But a big company with a hundred robots would make pork cheaper than I ever could.
S4.do: Gets the co-op to buy two or three robots and rent them to members, putting in five thousand of savings after Lucia talks him down from ten. Looks at selling higher-welfare pork direct, where big companies can't follow.
S4.feel: Alarmed and excited at once, like riding a bike downhill with no brakes.
S4.quote: I farm because I like being in the shed with the pigs, I don't want to farm from my phone.
S4.fieldNote: The most tech-friendly farmer admitted the thing that frightens him is being reduced to checking a screen. His instinct is to move first, through the co-op, but his wife acts as the brake on his risk-taking. The amount he'd put in shrank from ten to five thousand once he pictured her reaction.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, because it could go brilliantly or end me, and it depends who owns them. What would help is public money for farm co-ops to buy robots together, and a law that we can repair them ourselves. That one matters more than people think.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask farmers what they enjoy, not just what they earn. I'd give up some money to keep my hands on the pigs. I don't think the people building this stuff understand that.

headlineQuote: I farm because I like being in the shed with the pigs, I don't want to farm from my phone.
portrait: Marco is a 43-year-old pig and arable farmer on Station Road, with four hundred finishing pigs, sixty hectares of wheat and beans, and a wife, Lucia, who's a hospital nurse. He uses AI every day and loves gadgets, but he wants the tools owned by farmer co-ops and repairable by farmers, not locked up by big companies. He moves through the scenarios with energy, using AI to check his processor's prices and offering jobs to laid-off office workers. In the robot scenario he'd move first through the co-op, yet admits his real fear is ending up farming from a screen.
biggestWorry: The fast robots scenario, because big pig companies with many robots could undercut him unless farmers own the robots together.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for farm co-ops to buy robots together and a law letting farmers repair their own machines.
